text: Monica Samille Lewinsky, born on July 23, 1973, is an American activist who gained international recognition in the late 1990s after U.S. President Bill Clinton admitted to having an affair with her during her time as a White House intern from 1995 to 1997. The affair and its consequences, including Clinton's impeachment, became known as the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal. Born in San Francisco, California, Lewinsky grew up in an affluent family in Los Angeles, living in Brentwood and later Beverly Hills. Her father, Bernard Lewinsky, an oncologist, is the son of German Jews who emigrated from Germany in the 1920s, first to El Salvador and then to the United States when he was 14. Her mother, Marcia Kay Vilensky, who uses the name Marcia Lewis, is an author who wrote the "gossip biography" The Private Lives of the Three Tenors in 1996. Her maternal grandfather, Samuel M. Vilensky, was a Lithuanian Jew, and her maternal grandmother, Bronia Poleshuk, was born in the British Concession of Tianjin, China, to a Russian Jewish family. Lewinsky’s parents divorced in 1988 and each remarried. The family attended Sinai Temple in Los Angeles, and Lewinsky attended Sinai Akiba Academy, affiliated with the Temple. For her primary education, she went to the John Thomas Dye School in Bel-Air and graduated from Beverly Hills High School after three years, transferring to Bel Air Prep (later Pacific Hills School), where she graduated in 1991. After high school, she attended Santa Monica College while working for the drama department at Beverly Hills High School and at a tie shop. Andy Bleiler, her former high school drama instructor, alleged they began a five-year affair in 1992. In 1993, she enrolled at Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, earning a bachelor's degree in psychology in 1995. With help from a family connection, she secured an unpaid summer internship in the office of White House chief of staff Leon Panetta in July 1995, later moving to a paid position in the White House Office of Legislative Affairs in December 1995. Lewinsky stated she had nine sexual encounters with President Bill Clinton in the Oval Office between November 1995 and March 1997, involving oral sex and other sexual acts but not intercourse. Clinton had previously faced allegations from Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee, who filed a civil lawsuit alleging sexual harassment. Lewinsky’s name surfaced during the discovery phase of Jones' case as part of a pattern of inappropriate relationships. In April 1996, her superiors transferred her from the White House to the Pentagon, citing excessive time spent with Clinton. At the Pentagon, she worked as an assistant to chief spokesman Kenneth Bacon. In September 1997, after telling co-worker Linda Tripp about her relationship with Clinton, Tripp began secretly recording their conversations. Lewinsky left the Pentagon in December 1997 and submitted an affidavit in the Paula Jones case denying any physical relationship with Clinton. She attempted to persuade Tripp to lie under oath, but Tripp gave the tapes to Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr, expanding his investigation into the Whitewater controversy and the Jones case. Tripp reported the tapes to literary agent Lucianne Goldberg and convinced Lewinsky to save gifts Clinton gave her and not to dry clean a blue dress stained with Clinton's semen. Under oath, Clinton denied having a "sexual affair," "sexual relations," or "a sexual relationship" with Lewinsky. On January 26, 1998, Clinton stated during a nationally televised White House news conference, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," which sparked widespread media coverage. Lewinsky then hid from public attention at her mother's residence in the Watergate complex. News of her affair with Andy Bleiler also emerged, and he provided Starr with souvenirs, photographs, and documents sent by Lewinsky. Clinton later claimed, "There is not a sexual relationship, an improper sexual relationship or any other kind of improper relationship," which he defended in August 1998 as truthful due to the use of the present tense, arguing it depended on the meaning of the word "is." Starr obtained a blue dress with Clinton's semen stained on it and testimony that Clinton had inserted a cigar into Lewinsky’s vagina. Clinton denied perjury, citing that the legal definition of oral sex was not included in "sex" and that certain acts were performed on him, not by him, thus he did not engage in sexual relations. However, Lewinsky’s testimony to the Starr Commission contradicted Clinton’s claim of being entirely passive. Both Clinton and Lewinsky were called before a grand jury; Clinton testified via closed-circuit television, while Lewinsky testified in person and was granted transactional immunity by the Office of the Independent Counsel in exchange for her testimony. Her immunity agreement restricted public discussion, but she cooperated with Andrew Morton in writing her biography, Monica's Story, which was published in March 1999 and featured as a cover story in Time magazine. On March 3, 1999, Barbara Walters interviewed her on ABC's 20/20, watched by 70 million Americans, a record for a news show. Lewinsky earned about $500,000 from the book and $1 million from international rights to the interview, but faced high legal bills and living costs. In June 1999, Ms. magazine published articles by Susan Jane Gilman, Susie Bright, and Abiola Abrams discussing whether Lewinsky’s behavior had meaning for feminism. In 1999, Lewinsky declined to sign an autograph, saying, "I'm kind of known for something that's not so great to be known for." She made a cameo appearance on two sketches during the May 8, 1999, episode of NBC's Saturday Night Live. In September 1999, she began selling a line of handbags under the company name The Real Monica, Inc., sold online and at Henri Bendel in New York, Fred Segal in California, and The Cross in London. She designed the bags, described as "hippie-ish, reversible totes," and traveled to supervise their manufacture in Louisiana. In early 2000, she began appearing in television commercials for Jenny Craig, Inc., a $1 million endorsement deal requiring her to lose 40 or more pounds in six months. Despite her desire for a private life, she needed the money to pay legal fees and believed in the product. A Jenny Craig spokesperson said she represented a busy, active woman with weight struggles, reflecting many American women. The campaign was controversial, with some franchises switching to older ads, and the company stopped running the ads in February 2000, concluding the campaign in April 2000 and paying her only $300,000 of the $1 million. In early 2000, she moved to New York City, lived in the West Village, and became an A-list guest in the Manhattan social scene. In February 2000, she appeared on MTV's The Tom Green Show, where the host took her to his parents' home in Ottawa to find fabric for her handbag business. Later in 2000, she worked as a correspondent for Channel 5 in the UK on the show Monica's Postcards, reporting on U.S. culture and trends. In March 2002, no longer bound by her immunity agreement, she appeared in the HBO special "Monica in Black and White," part of the America Undercover series, where she answered audience questions about her life and the Clinton affair. In 2003, she hosted the reality television dating program Mr. Personality on Fox Television Network, advising young women contestants selecting men behind masks. Some Americans organized a boycott of advertisers on the show, but it debuted to very high ratings, and Alessandra Stanley of The New York Times noted it was a fitting niche for her. That year, she also appeared on V Graham Norton in the UK, High Chaparall in Sweden, and The View and Jimmy Kimmel Live! in the U.S. After Clinton's 2004 autobiography, My Life, appeared, Lewinsky said in an interview with the Daily Mail that he had lied and was a revisionist of history, claiming he had not corrected false statements made to protect his presidency. She stated the relationship was mutual and that while Clinton took advantage of her, it was consensual. By 2005, she found it difficult to escape the spotlight, which affected her professional and personal life. She stopped selling her handbag line and moved to London to study social psychology at the London School of Economics, graduating in December 2006 with a Master of Science degree, with a thesis titled "In Search of the Impartial Juror: An Exploration of the Third-Person Effect and Pre-Trial Publicity." For the next decade, she tried to avoid publicity. In 2009, she corresponded with scholar Ken Gormley, writing that Clinton had lied under oath when asked specific questions about their relationship. In 2013, items associated with Lewinsky that Andy Bleiler had turned over to Starr were auctioned by Bleiler's ex-wife. During her decade out of the public eye, she lived in London, Los Angeles, New York, and Portland but struggled to find employment in communications and marketing roles at nonprofit organizations. In May 2014, she wrote an essay for Vanity Fair titled "Shame and Survival," discussing her life and the scandal. She maintained the relationship was mutual and that while Clinton took advantage of her, it was consensual, and stated she deeply regretted what happened. She said it was time to "stick my head above the parapet" to reclaim her narrative and give purpose to her past. Vanity Fair later named her a contributor, stating she would contribute to their website on an ongoing basis. In July 2014, she was interviewed in a three-part television special for the National Geographic Channel, titled The 90s: The Last Great Decade, marking her first such interview in over ten years. In October 2014, she took a public stand against cyberbullying, calling herself "patient zero" of online harassment. Speaking at a Forbes "30 Under 30" summit, she said, "Having survived myself, what I want to do now is help other victims of the shame game survive, too," citing the suicide of Tyler Clementi as influential and joining Twitter to support her efforts. In March 2015, she delivered a TED talk calling for a more compassionate Internet. In June 2015, she became an ambassador and strategic advisor for the anti-bullying organization Bystander Revolution and gave an anti-cyberbullying speech at the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity. In September 2015, she was interviewed by Amy Robach on Good Morning America about Bystander Revolution's Month of Action campaign. She wrote the foreword to an October 2017 book by Sue Scheff and Melissa Schorr, Shame Nation: The Global Epidemic of Online Hate. In October 2017, she tweeted the #MeToo hashtag to indicate she was a victim of sexual harassment or assault without providing details. In her March 2018 Vanity Fair essay, she explained that while the relationship was consensual, due to Clinton being 27 years older and in a position of significant power, it constituted an "abuse of power" on his part, and she had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder as a result. In May 2018, she was disinvited from an event hosted by Town & Country when Bill Clinton accepted an invitation. In September 2018, she spoke at a conference in Jerusalem and, during a Q&A with journalist Yonit Levi, refused to answer whether Clinton owed her a private apology, walking off stage after the question was posed in a pre-event meeting. She later tweeted that the question was off-limits and that Levi honored her requests. A spokesman for Israel Television News Company confirmed Levi had kept all agreements with Lewinsky. In 2019, she was interviewed by John Oliver on Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, discussing the problem of public shaming and how her situation might have been different if social media had existed during the 1990s scandal. On August 6, 2019, it was announced that the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal was the subject of a new documentary.

Lewinsky was disinvited from an event hosted by Town & Country when Bill Clinton accepted an invitation to the event. In September 2018, Lewinsky spoke at a conference in Jerusalem, where she sat for a Q&A session with host journalist Yonit Levi. The first question Levi asked was whether Lewinsky thinks that Clinton owes her a private apology; Lewinsky refused to answer and walked off the stage. She later tweeted that the question was posed in a pre-event meeting with Levi, and she had told Levi that such a question was off limits. A spokesman for the Israel Television News Company, which hosted the conference and is Levi's employer, responded that Levi had kept all the agreements she made with Lewinsky and honored her requests. In 2019, she was interviewed by John Oliver on his HBO show Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, where they discussed the importance of solving the problem of public shaming and how her situation may have been different if social media had existed at the time that the scandal broke in the late 1990s. On August 6, 2019, it was announced that the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal would be the focus of the third season of the television series American Crime Story with the title Impeachment. The season began production in October 2020. Lewinsky was a co-producer. The season consists of 10 episodes and premiered on September 7, 2021. The season portrays the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and is based on the book A Vast Conspiracy: The Real Story of the Sex Scandal That Nearly Brought Down a President by Jeffrey Toobin. The 28-year-old actress Beanie Feldstein plays Monica Lewinsky. In discussing the series and her observations on social media and cancel culture today in an interview with Kara Swisher for the New York Times Opinion podcast Sway, Lewinsky noted: "I think that the first thing that went out the door in 1998 was the truth, and the second was context. And there’s no nuance. And we were all women who were thrust into the spotlight underneath a political film or sheen. And we were all reduced. We were all reduced in different ways to serve purposes for other people, for either political points or to make money." In October 2021, she was executive producer of an HBO documentary 15 Minutes of Shame, directed by Max Joseph, which focused on public shaming, online shaming, and ostracism. Lewinsky started her own production company, Alt Ending Productions, and signed a first look deal with 20th Television in June 2021. In February 2025, she launched her podcast, Reclaiming with Monica Lewinsky.
